Alex — thanks for the clear summary, that helps a lot. Short answer up front: we recommend a hybrid baseline+burst approach so you get cost-efficient steady-state with guaranteed headroom for your large-context/peak flows. I'll outline a concrete plan below and Karthik/Dev can add ops-level notes.

Proposed 3-line plan (high level):
1) Baseline pool: L4 instances sized to meet steady-state p50/p90 traffic (cost-effective, low per-token $).
2) Burst reserve: H100-backed slots as a secondary pool for p99/large-context/analytical jobs (opt for reserved H100 capacity sized to cover 95th-99th percentile peaks for queries that need large context).
3) Memory-heavy fallthrough: keep A100 (80GB) as a targeted fallback for jobs that absolutely need >40GB model memory (e.g., full 8k+ context with large weights unquantized). Use automatic model routing based on token length + model fingerprint.

Next steps I suggest: share a 72-hour trace (latency + token histogram), and we'll run a quick 48-hour pilot with L4 baseline + staged H100 burst routing. I've attached a short note with the initial SKU rationale.

Subject: INTERNAL: Notes on H100/A100/L4 tradeoffs for Nimbus

Internal thread — Dev here with a quick ops/telemetry perspective to feed into the customer plan. High-level tradeoffs and concrete knobs: 

H100 (pro): highest single-GPU throughput for FP16/FP8 kernels, great for high-concurrency and very low tail latency when batched well; good for large quantized models when you need performance headroom.
H100 (con): expensive on a per-GPU-hour basis; memory per card typical (80GB) but application-level available memory varies with multi-tenant runtime overhead.

A100 80GB (pro): best pure-memory option for unquantized large models and for workloads that require >40GB contiguous memory (8k+ context with large embedding tables or non-quantized weights). Predictable latency if model fits in memory.
A100 (con): lower peak FLOPs vs H100; can be cheaper than H100 for pure-memory use cases but worse for throughput-heavy quantized models.

L4 (pro): very cost-effective for steady-state token work, excellent price/perf on small-to-medium models, fast cold-starts in our runtime; good for synchronous 200ms SLO at typical token sizes when model is quantized and caching is effective.
L4 (con): limited memory (24GB-ish effective), not suitable for highest-concurrency large-context jobs.

Operational recommendations:
- Fleet mix: baseline 70% L4, 20% H100 reserve (reserved slots for peak), 10% A100-on-demand for specific memory jobs. This is a starting heuristic — we should tune to Nimbus traces.
- Routing policy: route by predicted token length + model tag. If predicted context > 6k tokens, route to H100/A100 path; for <2k tokens route to L4.
- Cache-first strategy: leverage prefix/KV cache aggressively; if a request hits cached KV pages it should stay on L4 path where possible.
- Quantization profile: recommend FP8/INT8 for steady-state L4 models; leave A100/H100 for FP16 or mixed-precision where precision must be preserved.
- Failover: when H100 capacity constrained, implement A100 fallthrough before degrading to L4 with graceful QoS (throttling + prioritized routing for latency-sensitive flows).

Attachments I ran locally: cost_model_3yr.xlsx, burst-routing-diagram.png (ops view).

Karthik, any additions on model-quality/regression risk?

Alex — circling back with the recommended mutual action plan and concrete numbers so procurement can move forward: 

Summary recommendation (concise):
- Baseline: 24 L4 slots sized to cover steady-state 95% traffic (est. 120M tokens/day) — cost-optimal for quantized models and cached hits.
- Burst reserve: 6 reserved H100 slots to cover p99 peaks and large-context analytics (automatically scaled into route when queue depth or predicted cost per request exceeds threshold).
- Memory-critical fallback: 2 A100-80GB on standby (on-demand billing) for jobs that cannot be quantized or require >40GB.

Why this mix: L4 handles the majority of short, cacheable requests within your 200ms p99 target when models are quantized and KV cache is hit. H100 gives predictable headroom for the tail and large batched workloads. A100 only used where memory is the gating factor.

Mutual action plan (attach):
1) Customer sends 72-hour telemetry + sample traces by 2025-09-19 (Alex).
2) Redwood runs a 48-hour pilot (L4 baseline + staged H100 burst) starting 2025-09-22. Redwood provides pilot dashboards and cost projection within 48 hours of pilot end.
3) Procurement proposal (reserved H100 slots + baseline L4 commit) drafted by Redwood by 2025-10-02.
4) Decision/contracting meeting on 2025-10-08.

Proposed procurement ask (rough): 6 reserved H100 slots (12-month commit) + baseline L4 commit equivalent to 24 slots. We can break these into phased reservations to reduce upfront spend. Exact slots and term to be adjusted after pilot.
